I have all the grounded evidence needed. Here is the incident report.

---

# Incident Report — MTA-2026-01-31

## 1. Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** | DHCP Request/ACK, all subsequent traffic |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** (Intel NIC) | ARP replies from 10.1.21.58, DHCP frames 1/3 |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | DHCP Option 12 (frames 1, 3), NBNS registrations, Kerberos `host/desktop-es9f3ml.win11office.com` SPN |
| AD domain | WIN11OFFICE.COM (NetBIOS: WIN11OFFICE) | Kerberos realm field, LDAP/CLDAP SRV lookups |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos `CNameString` on AS-REQ/TGS-REQ exchanges between 10.1.21.58 ↔ 10.1.21.2 (domain controller) |

Note: NBNS also advertises the alias `WIN11OFFICE` for the same machine — this is the NetBIOS *domain* name coincidentally resembling a hostname; the actual computer name (confirmed via DHCP option 12 and Kerberos SPN) is **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML**. 10.1.21.2 is the domain controller (WIN-LU4L24X3UB7.win11office.com).

## 2. Malware Family / Attribution

**Attribution: BEHAVIORAL, not signature-confirmed.** No IDS/Suricata alert file was provided alongside the pcap, and no executable payload was recoverable in cleartext (searched for MZ/PE headers and used `--export-objects http`; only HTML/JSON/ICO objects were transferred over plaintext HTTP — the rest of the suspicious traffic is TLS-encrypted, so no file hash can be computed from this evidence).

Based on the observed behavior chain, this is consistent with a **ClickFix/fake-download traffic-distribution-system (TDS) infection chain leading into a browser-fingerprinting stealer gate** (the specific C2 API shape — `/api/set_agent` with an `id`/`token` bot identifier and an `act=log` call that uploads a large JSON blob of canvas, WebGL, audio, font, screen, and hardware fingerprint data — most closely matches publicly reported **Katz Stealer** gate behavior). I cannot confirm this name via signature/hash because no AV/IDS detection or sample was available; treat the family name as a best-effort behavioral judgment, not a certainty.

**Observed infection sequence (all times relative to capture start):**
1. t=45.18s — victim host queries `www.google.com` (search).
2. t=45.98s — immediately pivots to `media.megafilehub4.lat` (104.21.48.156) — fake file-hosting domain, classic malvertising/search-poisoning redirect pattern.
3. t=48.36s — DNS lookup for `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` (104.21.46.67) — resolved but no subsequent connection observed.
4. t=90.55s — connects to `whooptm.cyou` (62.72.32.156).
5. t=92.34s–122.55s — connects to `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49) on **both TCP/443 and TCP/80**. This is where the fingerprinting/logging gate activity occurs (detailed below).
6. t=123.01s — `holiday-forever.cc` (80.97.160.24).
7. t=126.58s — `communicationfirewall-security.cc` (104.21.9.36 / 172.67.141.109) — name is consistent with a fake "security verification"/CAPTCHA-style lure page.
8. No further contact with any of these domains/IPs occurs for the remainder of the ~624-second capture — consistent with a single infection/check-in burst rather than sustained beaconing (a longer capture would be needed to confirm periodic C2).

## 3. Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in the pcap)

### Command-and-control endpoint
- **`whitepepper.su` — 153.92.1.49:80 and 153.92.1.49:443** (nginx/1.29.1) — the confirmed logging/fingerprinting gate.

### Malicious / suspicious domains (with resolved IPs)
| Domain | Resolved IP(s) |
|---|---|
| whitepepper.su | 153.92.1.49 |
| whooptm.cyou | 62.72.32.156 |
| holiday-forever.cc | 80.97.160.24 |
| communicationfirewall-security.cc | 104.21.9.36, 172.67.141.109 |
| media.megafilehub4.lat | 104.21.48.156, 172.67.154.67 |
| arch.filemegahab4.sbs | 104.21.46.67, 172.67.136.13 (DNS-resolved only, no connection observed) |
| hiyter.com | 104.21.22.231, 172.67.207.145 |

### Malicious URLs (captured in cleartext HTTP)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST — 8023-byte body: JSON with `platform`, `userAgent`, WebGL renderer/vendor, canvas fingerprint (base64 PNG), screen resolution 1920×1080, fonts list, hardware concurrency 12, network connection info)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log` (POST — 7975-byte body, same fingerprint structure)
- `http://whitepepper.su/favicon.ico` (2 requests, both 404)

Bot identifier observed in all requests: **id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C**, **token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b**

### Transferred files / hashes
**None recoverable.** All plaintext HTTP objects exported from the capture were benign (`connecttest.txt`, a Google time-sync JSON response, `favicon.ico`, and the fingerprint-log request/response bodies themselves — no `.exe`/`.dll`/`.zip`/script payload). A full-capture search for PE headers (`MZ` + "This program cannot be run in DOS mode") returned no hits. Traffic to `media.megafilehub4.lat`, `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`, `whooptm.cyou`, `holiday-forever.cc`, and `communicationfirewall-security.cc` was entirely TLS-encrypted, so if a payload was delivered on this leg it cannot be extracted or hashed from this pcap alone.

## 4. Recommendation
Given the encrypted gaps in the chain, this network evidence alone cannot confirm whether a second-stage payload actually executed on DESKTOP-ES9F3ML. Recommend host-based triage of that endpoint (process list, Prefetch, scheduled tasks, `HKCU\...\Run` keys, and browser download history for user gwyatt) to recover any dropped executable and obtain a hash for signature confirmation, and block the IOCs above at the perimeter/DNS layer.
